concept.overview: Jenkins is the most widely deployed open-source automation server, used to build, test, and deliver software through pipelines-as-code. You define a pipeline in a Jenkinsfile — a text file kept in your repository — and Jenkins executes its stages on a fleet of build agents whenever code changes. Its defining strength is an enormous plugin ecosystem (1,800+) that integrates with virtually every SCM, build tool, cloud, and notification system, making it the flexible glue of countless CI/CD setups.
concept.whyItMatters: Jenkins turns manual, error-prone release steps into a repeatable, auditable pipeline. It is the automation backbone in a huge share of enterprises, especially where self-hosting, on-prem builds, or deep customization are required. Knowing Jenkins — declarative pipelines, agents, credentials, and shared libraries — is a core, frequently-tested DevOps skill.
useCases: Running build/test pipelines automatically on every commit or pull request
Orchestrating multi-stage delivery: build → test → scan → deploy with approvals
Distributing builds across many agents (Linux, Windows, containers) for scale
Integrating tools — SonarQube, Nexus/Artifactory, Docker, Kubernetes — via plugins
Scheduling periodic jobs (nightly builds, backups, report generation)
concept.architecture: Jenkins uses a controller/agent model. The controller (formerly 'master') schedules jobs, stores configuration and build history, serves the web UI, and dispatches work; it should not run heavy builds itself. Agents (formerly 'slaves') are worker nodes — VMs, physical hosts, or dynamically provisioned containers/Kubernetes pods — that execute pipeline steps and report results back. A pipeline is defined declaratively in a Jenkinsfile with stages and steps; the controller checks out the repo, runs each stage on an allocated agent, streams logs, and records artifacts and test results. Credentials are stored encrypted in the controller and injected into builds. Plugins extend every part: SCM triggers, build tools, cloud agents, and post-build notifications.

definitions.def: The central Jenkins server that schedules jobs, holds config/history, and serves the UI.
A worker that executes pipeline steps; connected to the controller over SSH/JNLP or spun up on demand.
A pipeline defined as code (declarative or scripted) checked into the repository.
A stage is a named phase (Build, Test); steps are the individual commands inside it.
Freestyle jobs are UI-configured; Pipeline jobs are code-defined and version-controlled (preferred).
A slot on an agent that runs one build at a time; agents can have multiple executors.
Reusable pipeline code (Groovy) shared across many Jenkinsfiles.

bestPractices: Define pipelines as code (Jenkinsfile) in the repo — never configure critical jobs only in the UI.
Keep the controller light: run builds on agents, not on the controller.
Store secrets in the Credentials store and inject with withCredentials; never hardcode them.
Factor shared logic into shared libraries to keep Jenkinsfiles DRY.
Back up JENKINS_HOME and pin plugin versions; test plugin upgrades in staging.
pitfalls: Running heavy builds on the controller, making Jenkins slow and fragile.
Snowflake freestyle jobs configured by clicking, with no version control or reviewability.
Plugin sprawl and unpinned upgrades that break pipelines unexpectedly.
Secrets echoed into build logs or committed in Jenkinsfiles.
No backup of JENKINS_HOME — losing all jobs, history, and credentials on disk failure.
cheatSheet: Declarative skeleton: pipeline { agent; stages { stage { steps } } }
Notify on failure: post { failure { mail to: 'team@x' } }

quiz.question: What is a Jenkinsfile?
options: A pipeline defined as code, stored in the repository
quiz.explanation: A Jenkinsfile defines the pipeline (declarative or scripted) and lives in version control.

quiz.question: In the controller/agent model, what should the controller avoid doing?
quiz.explanation: The controller schedules and coordinates; heavy builds belong on agents to keep it responsive.

quiz.question: Pipeline (as-code) jobs are generally preferred over freestyle jobs for critical work.
quiz.explanation: Pipelines are version-controlled, reviewable, and reproducible; freestyle jobs are UI-only snowflakes.

quiz.question: How should database credentials be used in a pipeline?
options: Stored in Credentials and injected via withCredentials
quiz.explanation: Secrets live in the encrypted Credentials store and are injected into a scoped block.

quiz.question: Which block runs steps based on whether the build succeeded or failed?
quiz.explanation: The post section defines success/failure/always handlers.

quiz.question: You need a human to approve before deploying to production. Which step?
quiz.explanation: The input step pauses the pipeline until someone approves.

quiz.question: Shared libraries let multiple Jenkinsfiles reuse common pipeline code.
quiz.explanation: Shared libraries (Groovy) centralize reusable steps and keep pipelines DRY.

quiz.question: What primarily gives Jenkins its broad integrations?
quiz.explanation: 1,800+ plugins integrate Jenkins with SCMs, build tools, clouds, and more.

quiz.question: A disk failure wiped the Jenkins server and all jobs/history are gone. Root cause of the pain?
quiz.explanation: JENKINS_HOME holds jobs, history, and credentials; without backups it is unrecoverable.

quiz.question: What does 'agent { docker 'node:20' }' do for a stage?
options: Runs the stage inside a node:20 container
quiz.explanation: It executes the stage's steps inside the specified container image.

quiz.question: What is an executor in Jenkins?
options: A slot on an agent that runs one build at a time
quiz.explanation: Executors are concurrent build slots on an agent; more executors = more parallel builds.

quiz.question: Pipelines keep breaking after routine plugin updates. Best practice to reduce this?
options: Pin plugin versions and test upgrades in staging
quiz.explanation: Pinning versions and testing upgrades prevents surprise breakage in production pipelines.

quiz.question: Which of these is the recommended way to restrict what each Jenkins user can do?
options: Give everyone admin and rely on trust
Enable an authorization strategy such as Role-Based Strategy and assign scoped roles
quiz.explanation: Enable a security realm for authentication plus an authorization strategy (e.g. Role-Based Strategy) to grant least-privilege permissions.

quiz.question: What is 'self-testing code' in a CI context?
options: Code shipped with an automated test suite the pipeline runs on every change
Code that tests itself in production only
quiz.explanation: Self-testing code ships with automated tests CI executes on every commit, so regressions surface immediately.

guides.title: User Management
guides.intro: Add users to Jenkins and control what each one can do using the Role-Based Authorization Strategy. Screenshots are loaded from /guides/jenkins/*.png; until you add them, an illustrative diagram of each step is shown instead.

steps.text: Navigate to Jenkins → Manage Jenkins → Users.
steps.caption: Manage Jenkins → Users

steps.text: On the Users page click + Create User, then fill in the user ID, name, password, and email, and click Create User. Repeat for each user (here: Dev, Devops, jenkins, QA).
steps.caption: Jenkins' own user database — + Create User

steps.text: Roles require a plugin. Go to Manage Jenkins → Plugins → Available plugins, search for "Role-based Authorization Strategy", install it, and restart Jenkins if prompted.
steps.caption: Install the Role-based Authorization Strategy plugin

steps.text: Go to Manage Jenkins → Security. Under Authentication you will see Authorization set to "Logged-in users can do anything".
steps.caption: Authorization → Logged-in users can do anything

steps.text: Change Authorization to "Role-Based Strategy" and click Save.
steps.caption: Authorization → Role-Based Strategy

steps.text: A new option, "Manage and Assign Roles", now appears under Manage Jenkins → Security.
steps.caption: The new Manage and Assign Roles entry

steps.text: Open Manage Roles and add global roles (for example Developer, Testing, DevOps), ticking the permissions each role should have, then Save.
steps.caption: Manage Roles — global roles & permissions

steps.text: Open Assign Roles and map each user to a role (for example DevOps Engineer → DevOps, Testing Team → Testing, Developer → Developer), then Save.
steps.caption: Assign roles to the created users

steps.text: Open Jenkins in an incognito / private browser window and sign in as one of the users you created (for example dev).
steps.caption: Sign in to Jenkins (incognito)

steps.text: Confirm the user only sees and can do what their assigned role allows.
steps.caption: Signed in — role-limited view
